title: Kafka: retries, performance and retention
seriesDescription: A Kafka deep dive for system design interviews: why Kafka exists, terminology, messages and keys, offsets and replication, when to use it, scalability, hot partitions, fault tolerance, retries, performance and retention.
description: Producer retries and idempotence, consumer retry topics and DLQs, batching, compression, key choice and retention.
source: Study notes: Kafka deep dive for system design interviews

questions.prompt: Why combine producer retries with idempotent mode?

options.text: Retries protect against loss; idempotence stops a retried send from storing the message twice.
options.why: Right: say them together.

options.text: Idempotence makes retries unnecessary in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Both are needed; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Retries make messages smaller as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Not their effect; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Idempotence deletes duplicates in the consumer without any extra configuration.
options.why: It acts at the producer and broker.

questions.explanation: Retry alone can write the message twice if the first send actually worked.

questions.prompt: Kafka has no built-in consumer retries. What is the common pattern?

options.text: On failure, move the message to a retry topic with its own consumer, and after too many attempts to a dead letter queue.
options.why: Right: failures do not block healthy traffic.

options.text: Block the main consumer until the message succeeds under normal operating conditions.
options.why: That stalls everything behind it.

options.text: Delete failed messages in a typical production setup as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: You would lose them; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Ask Kafka to retry automatically forever for most everyday workloads.
options.why: It does not; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: In the Web Crawler breakdown SQS is chosen to get retries and a DLQ without building them.

questions.prompt: What is a dead letter queue for?

options.text: Keeping messages that failed too many times for later investigation.
options.why: Right: a place for failures.

options.text: Speeding up healthy messages as a general rule of thumb in the majority of deployments.
options.why: Unrelated; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Replacing the main topic.
options.why: It is a side place; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Storing all successful messages for most everyday workloads under normal operating conditions.
options.why: It holds failures; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: A separate topic lets you retry as often as you like without slowing the main consumer.

questions.prompt: What do batching and compression each reduce?

options.text: Batching cuts per-message overhead; compression cuts bytes on the wire.
options.why: Right: GZIP, Snappy, LZ4 are options.

options.text: Batching cuts bytes; compression cuts overhead without any extra configuration.
options.why: Swapped; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Both only affect retention.
options.why: They affect the network and overhead.

options.text: Both make ordering stronger in a typical production setup for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Not their purpose; it does not answer the question asked.

questions.explanation: sendBatch() can cover several topics at once.

questions.prompt: Arguably the largest performance impact in Kafka comes from what?

options.text: Your partition key: an even key gives maximum parallelism, a skewed key makes a bottleneck.
options.why: Right: fix the key first.

options.text: The colour of the logs.
options.why: Not real; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The number of console windows open in the majority of deployments without any extra configuration.
options.why: Not real; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: The programming language of the consumer only under normal operating conditions as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: Less important than the key.

questions.explanation: Everything else, like batching and compression, is tuning.

questions.prompt: What is Kafka's default retention for messages?

options.text: Seven days, after which older messages are removed.
options.why: Right: the default retention window.

options.text: One hour, because Kafka is meant for transient data.
options.why: Too short for the default.

options.text: Forever, unless an admin deletes the topic by hand.
options.why: Retention removes old data.

options.text: Until the first consumer has read the message once.
options.why: Reading does not delete.

questions.explanation: Retention decides how far back a consumer can replay.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about retention.

options.text: retention.ms sets a time limit.
options.why: Yes; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: retention.bytes sets a size limit.
options.why: Yes; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Longer retention costs more storage and can affect performance.
options.why: Yes: watch the cost; it does not answer the question asked.

options.text: Retention only applies to messages never read.
options.why: No: it applies regardless of reads.

questions.explanation: If asked to keep messages long, raise retention and mention the storage cost.

questions.prompt: True or false: turning on idempotent mode means a message is stored only once even when the producer wrongly thought a send failed.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: that is its purpose.

options.text: False
options.why: It is what idempotence is for.

questions.explanation: The broker recognises the repeated send and does not store a duplicate.
